description_full: IDT Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides fintech and communications solutions in the United States, the United Kingdom, and internationally. It operates in four segments: National Retail Solutions, Fintech, Net2phone, and Traditional Communications. The company operates point of sale, a terminal-based platform which provides independent retailers with store management software, electronic payment processing, and other ancillary merchant services; and marketers with retail media advertising and transaction data. It also offers BOSS Money for international money remittance, and related value and payment transfer services, as well as net2phone solutions comprising unified communications as a service; contact center as a service under the uContact brand; net2phone AI, which delivers customer experiences across sales, support, and administrative tasks; and net2phone Coach, a workforce intelligence and coaching platform. In addition, the company provides IDT Digital Payments, which enables businesses, entrepreneurs, and developers to offer prepaid digital offerings, including mobile airtime top-up, mobile data bundles, digital gift cards, and eSIMs through its Zendit platform; and BOSS Revolution, which offers international long-distance voice calling to immigrant communities. Further, it provides IDT Global, a wholesale provider of international voice, SMS termination, and outsourced traffic management solutions to telecoms; and IDT Express, a mobile self-service portal paired with dedicated account managers backed by customer support. IDT Corporation was incorporated in 1978 and is headquartered in Newark, New Jersey.

financial_summary: IDT Corporation is a mid-cap communication services business with a $2.1B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 75% against a 9% cost of capital — a 66-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $68M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.05× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 12% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Communication Services peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 9% operating margin is roughly in line with the Communication Services median (9%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.45x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+18.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 61% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.31 vs 5y 0.85), so read it loosely.
About $14.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 51% in the 2022 bear market and 97% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 4% below its DCF fair value of $86.73, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $66.76 to $115 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 24.0 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 13.9 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 30.4 vs 11.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 0% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $85.00 on average, 2% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 75% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 66pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.20).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.05x.
ROE of 23% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.0x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 4.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $219.1M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.6, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years, -2.2% over 5 years and -1.4% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 88% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 7% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 2%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 1.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 2, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 12.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 64%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (17 sales, net $3.8M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.3% (0.3% in dividends).
people: With about 1,965 employees, each generates about $661K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $1.4M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
